text:
First lady Melania Trump has worked quietly to push forward legislation and initiatives she cares about, according to her senior advisor.(Image: Getty Images )

Melania Trump's adviser spoke about her style of working, how it was different from her first administration, and the portfolio of issues she has taken under her wing this time around.

Marc Beckman told POLITICO in an interview that often, her initiatives have been met with skepticism, including when she tried to advocate for her 'Fostering the Future' legislation, that helped young people aging out of the foster care system.

Beckman said that Republican Jason Smith felt "fearful" about this step because “Democrats really don’t like her husband,” but the first lady pushed for it nevertheless. “I want this on Donald’s desk by the August recess," Beckman recalled Trump saying.

Beckman said that Trump cared little for how the media covered her term as first lady, especially after her husband's first term in the White House, where she believed the media covered them unfairly. Even in her memoir, Trump spoke about how she and her husband were surrounded by staff they didn’t believe were competent enough and ran into various public relations snafus.

“She doesn’t decide to do anything based on what the media might say,” Beckman said. “There’s so much important work that she’s doing.”

This time around, she has decided to focus on issues that relate to children, specifically ones that were victims of the war between Russia and Ukraine. Early in her second term, she wrote a letter to Russian President Vladimir Putin and helped arrange many Russian and Ukrainian reuniting with their parents.

“The images coming out where she learned about these children who were displaced as a result of the war really impacted her,” Beckman said.

He continued, “she and her representative are continuing forward with working toward getting as many children back with their families as she can, she’s very committed to it… she’s not looking at nations or borders” in her reunification efforts. The first lady's efforts in this initiative are ongoing, Beckman said.

The president praised his wife as “smart” and “hardworking" during an interview with POLITICO in March. "She’s got a great network of people that help her with returning children,” he said. “She’s done a great job. Not since Eleanor Roosevelt has there been anybody like her.”

Beckman also said that Trump's rare public appearances and interviews are intentional so that her statements on issues she cares about are more intentional.

Her other work includes hosting Cabinet officials and tech CEOs, including Google’s Sundar Pichai and IBM’s Arvind Krishna, to promote integrating artificial intelligence into children’s education.

She has also lent support to the Take It Down Act, singed into law in May, which deals with nonconsensual pictures and deepfakes published on the internet.
